ref: Contra Noetum 10 (ANF vol. 5 numbering; Lagarde 1858 chapter 10; Bonwetsch/Lagarde chapter numbers agree)
greek: θεὺς μόνος ὑπάρχων καὶ μηδὲν ἔχων ἑαυτῷ σύγχρονον, ἐβουλήθη κόσμον κτίσαι. [...] τῶν δὲ γινομένων ἀρχηγὸν καὶ σύμβουλον καὶ ἐργάτην ἐγέννα λόγον, ὃν λόγον ἔχων ἐν ἑαυτῷ ἀόρατόν τε ὄντα τῷ κτιζομένῳ κόσμῳ ὁρατὸν ποιεῖ, προτέραν φωνὴν φθεγγόμενος, καὶ φῶς ἐκ φωτὸς γεννῶν προῆκεν τῇ κτίσει κύριον τὸν ἴδιον νοῦν, αὐτῷ μόνῳ πρότερον ὁρατὸν ὑπάρχοντα
greek_edition: Lagarde, Hippolyti Romani quae feruntur omnia graece (Leipzig: Teubner, 1858), printed page as stated; OCR text layer checked against page scan (visually read on the PNG render). Scan source: https://archive.org/details/hippolytiromani00lagagoog Read visually on PNG render of PDF page 71 (printed 50) and 72 (printed 51).
english: God, subsisting alone, and having nothing contemporaneous with Himself, determined to create the world. [...] And as the Author, and fellow-Counsellor, and Framer of the things that are in formation, He begot the Word; and as He bears this Word in Himself, and that, too, as (yet) invisible to the world which is created, He makes Him visible; (and) uttering the voice first, and begetting Him as Light of Light, He set Him forth to the world as its Lord, (and) His own mind
translator: J.H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5, per New Advent footer; the brief names Salmond: discrepancy, see notes.md)
page: New Advent page 0521 has no print page; printed Lagarde p. 50-51
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1886), digitised by New Advent
what_it_says: Before creating, God 'begot' the Word as His own counsel, and set Him forth as Light of Light, his own mind, visible to the world.
limits: Hippolytus here gives an economic/manifestation scheme (the Word is made visible for salvation), not an eternal consubstantial generation; 'begot' and 'uttering the voice first' are read by critics as creation-linked (Arian-style emanation). Nicene answer needs the eternal-generation sense from Athanasius and Augustine.

ref: Contra Noetum 11 (ANF vol. 5; Lagarde 1858 chapter 11)
greek: καὶ οὕτως παρίστατο αὐτῷ ἕτερος. ἕτερον δὲ λέγων οὐ δύο θεοὺς λέγω, ἀλλ᾽ ὡς φῶς ἐκ φωτὸς ἢ ὡς ὕδωρ ἐκ πηγῆς ἢ ὡς ἀκτῖνα ἀπὸ ἡλίου. δύναμις γὰρ μία ἡ ἐκ τοῦ παντός, τὸ δὲ πᾶν πατήρ, ἐξ οὗ δύναμις λόγος. οὗτος δὲ νοῦς, ὃς προβὰς ἐν κόσμῳ ἐδείκνυτο παῖς θεοῦ.
greek_edition: Lagarde, Hippolyti Romani quae feruntur omnia graece (Leipzig: Teubner, 1858), printed page as stated; OCR text layer checked against page scan (visually read on the PNG render). Scan source: https://archive.org/details/hippolytiromani00lagagoog Read visually on PNG render of PDF page 72 (printed 51).
english: And thus there appeared another beside Himself. But when I say another, I do not mean that there are two Gods, but that it is only as light of light, or as water from a fountain, or as a ray from the sun. For there is but one power, which is from the All; and the Father is the All, from whom comes this Power, the Word. And this is the mind which came forth into the world, and was manifested as the Son of God.
translator: J.H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5, per New Advent footer)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5 (1886), via New Advent
what_it_says: Hippolytus says the second 'another' is not a second God but like light from light, water from a fountain, or a ray from the sun, from one power.
limits: The analogies (ray, water, derived light) are what Arian and subordinationist readers exploit; Nicene reading needs 'light of light' from the Creed and Augustine. 'Came forth' is the same verb as the brief's 'went forth'.

ref: Contra Noetum 7 (ANF vol. 5; Lagarde 1858 chapter 7)
greek: ἐπεὶ δύο πρόσωπα ἔδειξεν, δύναμιν δὲ μίαν. αὐτὸς δὲ αὐτὸ ἐπέλυσεν, εἰπὼν περὶ μαθητῶν πρὸς τὸν πατέρα· τὴν δόξαν, ἣν ἔδωκάς μοι, ἔδωκα αὐτοῖς, ἵνα ὦσιν ἓν, καθὼς ἡμεῖς ἕν.
greek_edition: Lagarde, Hippolyti Romani quae feruntur omnia graece (Leipzig: Teubner, 1858), printed page as stated; OCR text layer checked against page scan (visually read on the PNG render). Scan source: https://archive.org/details/hippolytiromani00lagagoog Only the OCR text layer (PDF page 70, printed 49) was read; the scan was not viewed for this line; OCR reads ζ for ξ in this printing (ἔδειζεν) and the form is normalised here to ἔδειξεν. Greek must be re-checked on the scan.
english: For the word are is not said of one person, but it refers to two persons, and one power. He has Himself made this clear, when He spoke to His Father concerning the disciples, The glory which You gave me I have given them; that they may be one, even as we are one
translator: J.H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5, per New Advent footer)
page: printed Lagarde p. 49 (Greek); ANF page unknown
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5 (1886), via New Advent; Lagarde 1858
what_it_says: Hippolytus reads John 10:30 'we are one' (plural 'are') as two persons with one power.
limits: 'Two persons with one power' is Hippolytus's own formula; he does not yet say one substance. Critics (Arian and Unitarian) read the 'one power' as moral unity; Nicene reading needs one ousia, which Hippolytus does not state here.

ref: Contra Noetum 8 (ANF vol. 5; Lagarde 1858 chapter 8)
greek: ὅτι μία δύναμις τούτου, καὶ ὅσον μὲν κατὰ τὴν δύναμιν, εἷς ἐστι θεός, ὅσον δὲ κατὰ τὴν οἰκονομίαν, τριχῆς ἡ ἐπίδειξις, ὡς ὕστερον ἀποδειχθήσεται.
greek_edition: Lagarde, Hippolyti Romani quae feruntur omnia graece (Leipzig: Teubner, 1858), printed page as stated; OCR text layer checked against page scan (visually read on the PNG render). Scan source: https://archive.org/details/hippolytiromani00lagagoog Read visually on PNG render of PDF page 71 (printed 50), top of page.
english: As far as regards the power, therefore, God is one. But as far as regards the economy there is a threefold manifestation, as shall be proved afterwards when we give account of the true doctrine.
translator: J.H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5, per New Advent footer)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5 (1886), via New Advent
what_it_says: God is one as to power; as to the economy there is a threefold manifestation.
limits: The power/economy split makes the threefold distinction a matter of manifestation, a formula that Sabellians and later Nicene writers (Athanasius) criticised; it does not yet affirm three hypostases.

ref: Contra Noetum 14 (ANF vol. 5; Lagarde 1858 chapter 14)
greek: δύο μὲν οὐκ ἐρῶ θεοὺς ἀλλ᾽ ἢ ἕνα, πρόσωπα δὲ δύο, οἰκονομίᾳ δὲ τρίτην τὴν χάριν τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος. πατὴρ μὲν γὰρ εἷς, πρόσωπα δὲ δύο, ὅτι καὶ ὁ υἱός, τὸ δὲ τρίτον τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα. πατὴρ ἐντέλλεται, λόγος ἀποτελεῖ, υἱὸς δὲ δείκνυται, δι᾽ οὗ πατὴρ πιστεύεται.
greek_edition: Lagarde, Hippolyti Romani quae feruntur omnia graece (Leipzig: Teubner, 1858), printed page as stated; OCR text layer checked against page scan (visually read on the PNG render). Scan source: https://archive.org/details/hippolytiromani00lagagoog Read visually on PNG render of PDF page 73 (printed 52) and page 74 (printed 53).
english: I shall not indeed speak of two Gods, but of one; of two Persons however, and of a third economy (disposition), viz., the grace of the Holy Ghost. For the Father indeed is One, but there are two Persons, because there is also the Son; and then there is the third, the Holy Spirit. The Father decrees, the Word executes, and the Son is manifested, through whom the Father is believed on.
translator: J.H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5, per New Advent footer)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5 (1886), via New Advent
what_it_says: One God, two Persons (Father and Son), and a third economy of the Holy Spirit; the Father commands, the Word executes.
limits: The brief's 'two persons' is the hard phrase: it looks numerical (two Persons = two beings) and the ordering 'Father decrees, Word executes' is subordinationist in form. Hippolytus has no homoousios; Nicene answer is the later distinction ousia/hypostasis (Basil Ep. 236 s.6). Scholars (Kelly, Hanson) read this as pre-Nicene economic language.

ref: Contra Noetum 15 (ANF vol. 5; Lagarde 1858 chapter 15)
greek: ποῖον οὖν υἱὸν ἑαυτοῦ ὁ θεὸς διὰ τῆς σαρκὸς κατέπεμψεν ἀλλ᾽ ἢ τὸν λόγον; ὃν υἱὸν προσηγόρευε διὰ τὸ μέλλειν αὐτὸν γενέσθαι. [...] οὔτε γὰρ ἄσαρκος καὶ καθ᾽ ἑαυτὸν ὁ λόγος τέλειος ἦν υἱός (καίτοι τέλειος λόγος ὢν μονογενής), οὔτε ἡ σὰρξ καθ᾽ ἑαυτὴν δίχα τοῦ λόγου ὑποστῆναι ἠδύνατο διὰ τὸ ἐν λόγῳ τὴν σύστασιν ἔχειν. οὕτως οὖν εἷς υἱὸς τέλειος θεοῦ ἐφανερώθη.
greek_edition: Lagarde, Hippolyti Romani quae feruntur omnia graece (Leipzig: Teubner, 1858), printed page as stated; OCR text layer checked against page scan (visually read on the PNG render). Scan source: https://archive.org/details/hippolytiromani00lagagoog Read visually on PNG render of PDF page 75 (printed 54); text layer also present on that page.
english: What Son of His own, then, did God send through the flesh but the Word, whom He addressed as Son because He was to become such (or be begotten) in the future? [...] For neither was the Word, prior to incarnation and when by Himself, yet perfect Son, although He was perfect Word, only-begotten. Nor could the flesh subsist by itself apart from the Word, because it has its subsistence in the Word. Thus, then, one perfect Son of God was manifested.
translator: J.H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5, per New Advent footer)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5 (1886), via New Advent
what_it_says: The Word was addressed as Son only in view of the incarnation; before the incarnation the Word was Word and only-begotten but not yet 'perfect Son'.
limits: This is the main hard passage for 'Son only from incarnation' (Arian, Unitarian, Muslim and some scholarly readings). The text says the Word is 'only-begotten' before the flesh, so it does not deny eternal generation of the Word; but it denies that the Word was Son in the full sense before the incarnation. Nicene answer: Athanasius Or. c. Ar. 2.57, Dionysius of Rome (De Decretis 26). Greek 'ὃν υἱὸν' is OCR-read as 'Ov viv' and confirmed on the scan.

ref: Contra Noetum 12 (ANF vol. 5; Lagarde 1858 chapter 12) and 13
greek_edition: Greek not transcribed for this item (ch. 12 Greek is on Lagarde printed p. 51 and 52; not used).
english: Acting then in these (prophets), the Word spoke of Himself. For already He became His own herald, and showed that the Word would be manifested among men.
translator: J.H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5, per New Advent footer)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5 (1886), via New Advent
what_it_says: Before the incarnation the Word was already speaking through the prophets, showing He would be manifested.
limits: Used only for the context of ch. 15; Hippolytus's Logos is a manifestation of a pre-existent Word, which Nicene writers read as eternal generation.

ref: Contra Noetum 3 and 7 (ANF vol. 5 numbering)
greek_edition: Greek not transcribed here; Lagarde printed p. 44 (ch. 3) not visually read for this item.
english: For who will not say that there is one God? Yet he will not on that account deny the economy (i.e., the number and disposition of persons in the Trinity).
translator: J.H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5, per New Advent footer)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5 (1886), via New Advent
what_it_says: Hippolytus holds that one God is affirmed while the economy (number and order of persons) is also affirmed.
limits: The ANF footnote glosses 'economy' as 'number and disposition of persons'; the Greek word oikonomia is not glossed in the Greek.

ref: Contra Noetum (ANF) 10 with Lagarde 1858 title
greek: Ὁμιλία Ἱππολύτου εἰς τὴν αἵρεσιν Νοήτου τινός.
greek_edition: Lagarde, Hippolyti Romani quae feruntur omnia graece (Leipzig: Teubner, 1858), printed page as stated; OCR text layer checked against page scan (visually read on the PNG render). Scan source: https://archive.org/details/hippolytiromani00lagagoog Title read visually on PNG render of PDF page 64 (printed 43), item 3.
english: Homily of Hippolytus against the heresy of a certain Noetus (title only; ANF gives 'Against Noetus').
translator: ANF title (MacMahon page); Greek title is Lagarde's
edition: Lagarde 1858 (Greek) / Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5 (1886)
what_it_says: The work is titled as an address against the heresy of Noetus.
limits: Authorship disputed (Nautin, Brent): the Greek title does not settle who wrote it.

ref: Athanasius, De Decretis 15 (NPNF2 vol. 4, Newman)
greek_edition: Greek not consulted (PG 25). English only.
english: We have learned from divine Scripture, that the Son of God, as was said above, is the very Word and Wisdom of the Father. For the Apostle says, 'Christ the power of God and the Wisdom of God;' and John after saying, 'And the Word was made flesh,' at once adds, 'And we saw His glory, the glory as of the Only-begotten of the Father.'
translator: John Henry Newman
edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1892), digitised by New Advent
what_it_says: The Son is the very Word and Wisdom of the Father, so the Word is Only-begotten.
limits: Athanasius's argument is against Arians; it does not address Hippolytus's 'perfect Son only after incarnation' phrasing directly.

ref: Athanasius, De Decretis 26 (quotes Dionysius of Rome, letter against Sabellius and Marcion)
greek_edition: Greek not consulted (Athanasius, PG 25; Dionysius letter preserved in Athanasius, De sententia Dionysii 13-18). English only.
english: For if He came to be Son, once He was not; but He was always, if (that is) He be in the Father, as He says Himself, and if the Christ be Word and Wisdom and Power... If then the Son came into being, once these attributes were not; consequently there was a time, when God was without them; which is most absurd.
translator: John Henry Newman (translating Athanasius; the Dionysius letter is quoted within it)
edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892), via New Advent
what_it_says: Dionysius of Rome (3rd c.) says the Son cannot have 'come to be' Son, since Word, Wisdom and Power are eternal in the Father.
limits: Dionysius's letter survives only as quoted by Athanasius; the Greek is not checked here. It is a parallel to Hippolytus's Trinitarian language from the Roman church, not an explicit answer to C. Noet. 15.

ref: Athanasius, Discourses against the Arians 2.5 (NPNF2 vol. 4, Newman and Robertson)
greek_edition: Greek not consulted (PG 26). English only.
english: For a work could never be Son and Word; nor could the Son be a work. [...] it is proper to ask of them this first, whether He is Son and Word and Wisdom. For if this is shown, the surmise about work and creation falls to the ground at once and is ended.
translator: John Henry Newman and Archibald Robertson
edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892), via New Advent
what_it_says: A work cannot be Son and Word, so the Son is not a creature.
limits: Argument rests on the Arian premise that 'work' and 'Son' exclude each other; it does not address the Hippolytean sense of 'became Son'.

ref: Athanasius, Discourse II Against the Arians 57 (NPNF2 vol. 4)
greek_edition: Greek not consulted. English only.
english: For had He been a creature, He had not said, 'He begets me,' for the creatures are from without, and are works of the Maker; but the Offspring is not from without nor a work, but from the Father, and proper to His Essence. [...] Therefore the creatures began to be made; but the Word of God, not having beginning of being, certainly did not begin to be, nor begin to come to be, but was ever.
translator: John Henry Newman and Archibald Robertson
edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892), via New Advent
what_it_says: The Word did not begin to be; he was always, the Offspring of the Father, not a creature.
limits: Athanasius answers the question 'when did the Son begin?' from a Nicene premise that Hippolytus did not share in these words; it answers the 'Son only from incarnation' objection indirectly.

ref: Irenaeus, Against Heresies IV.20.3 (ANF vol. 1, Roberts and Rambaut)
greek_edition: Greek not extant for this book; Latin (Harvey 1857) not opened. English only.
english: I have also largely demonstrated, that the Word, namely the Son, was always with the Father; and that Wisdom also, which is the Spirit, was present with Him, anterior to all creation.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), via New Advent
what_it_says: The Word (the Son) was always with the Father, and Wisdom (the Spirit) was present before creation.
limits: Identifies Wisdom with the Spirit, which later Nicene language does not; Irenaeus's Latin is not checked.

ref: Irenaeus, Against Heresies IV.6.2 (ANF vol. 1)
greek_edition: Greek not extant for this book; Latin not opened. English only.
english: But if Christ did then [only] begin to have existence when He came [into the world] as man, and [if] the Father did remember [only] in the times of Tiberius Caesar to provide for [the wants of] men, and His Word was shown to have not always coexisted with His creatures; [it may be remarked that] neither then was it necessary that another God should be proclaimed.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), via New Advent
what_it_says: Irenaeus states the objection that the Son began at the incarnation and rejects its consequences.
limits: The sentence is a conditional that Irenaeus refutes (against Marcionites and Gnostics); it is not his own thesis, and it is quoted as an opponent's position in a polemical chain.

ref: Justin, Dialogue with Trypho 128 (ANF vol. 1, Dods and Reith)
greek_edition: Greek (Otto, Corpus Apologetarum) not consulted. English only.
english: I have discussed briefly in what has gone before; when I asserted that this power was begotten from the Father, by His power and will, but not by abscission, as if the essence of the Father were divided; as all other things partitioned and divided are not the same after as before they were divided: and, for the sake of example, I took the case of fires kindled from a fire.
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), via New Advent
what_it_says: The Word is begotten from the Father by His power and will, not by division of the Father's essence, like one fire kindled from another.
limits: Justin calls the Word numerically distinct and a 'power' sent forth; this is a second-century subordinationist frame (Word as second God), not Nicene; the fire analogy is an illustration.

ref: Theophilus, To Autolycus II.10 (ANF vol. 2, Dods)
greek_edition: Greek not consulted (Otto). English only.
english: God, then, having His own Word internal within His own bowels, begot Him, emitting Him along with His own wisdom before all things.
translator: Marcus Dods
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), via New Advent
what_it_says: God had the Word internal in Himself, and begot and emitted Him with His wisdom before creation.
limits: 'Emitting' is a prolation scheme (as in Hippolytus CN 10); Theophilus does not state eternal co-equal Son.

ref: Athenagoras, Plea for the Christians 10 (ANF vol. 2, Pratten)
greek_edition: Greek words νοῦς καὶ λόγος appear on the New Advent page; full Greek (Schwartz 1891) not consulted.
english: But the Son of God is the Logos of the Father, in idea and in operation; for after the pattern of Him and by Him were all things made, the Father and the Son being one. And, the Son being in the Father and the Father in the Son, in oneness and power of spirit, the understanding and reason (νοῦς καὶ λόγος) of the Father is the Son of God. [...] God, who is the eternal mind (νοῦς), had the Logos in Himself, being from eternity instinct with Logos.
translator: B.P. Pratten
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), via New Advent
what_it_says: The Son is the Father's Logos (reason) and the Father and Son are one; God had the Logos in Himself from eternity.
limits: Athenagoras also calls the Son 'the first product of the Father' and says He came forth as the idea of creation, which subordinationist readers cite; the eternal Logos clause is the one used for Nicene reading.

ref: Tertullian, Against Praxeas 2 (ANF vol. 3, Holmes)
greek_edition: Latin (Kroymann/Refoulé) not opened; the Greek oikonomia term appears in the English. English only.
english: The mystery of the dispensation... distributes the Unity into a Trinity, placing in their order the three Persons— the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost: three, however, not in condition, but in degree; not in substance, but in form; not in power, but in aspect; yet of one substance, and of one condition, and of one power.
translator: Peter Holmes
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (1885), via New Advent
what_it_says: Three persons in one Godhead, distinguished by degree, form and aspect but one substance and one power.
limits: 'Degree, form, aspect' sounds modalist to Nicene critics; Tertullian's Latin 'persona' and 'substantia' are not checked here. Hippolytus's 'two persons' is parallel but not identical.

ref: Tertullian, Against Praxeas 8 (ANF vol. 3)
greek_edition: Latin not opened. English only.
english: The Word, therefore, is both always in the Father... and never separate from the Father, or other than the Father, since I and the Father are one. [...] Where, however, there is a second, there must be two; and where there is a third, there must be three.
translator: Peter Holmes
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (1885), via New Advent
what_it_says: The Son is a prolation from the Father without separation; second implies two, third implies three.
limits: 'Prolation' (probolē) is the term Valentinians used; Tertullian explains it as non-separating. Tertullian's 'root/tree' analogy is the one Nicene readers replaced by eternal generation.

ref: Tertullian, Against Praxeas 9 (ANF vol. 3)
greek_edition: Latin not opened. English only.
english: For the Father is the entire substance, but the Son is a derivation and portion of the whole, as He Himself acknowledges: My Father is greater than I. John 14:28. [...] Thus the Father is distinct from the Son, being greater than the Son.
translator: Peter Holmes
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (1885), via New Advent
what_it_says: The Father is the whole substance, the Son a derivation and portion; the Father is greater.
limits: 'Portion' (portio) and 'greater' are subordinationist; Nicene theology rejects both (Athanasius, Or. 1; the Creed). Tertullian's answer (distinction not division) is only partial.

ref: Tertullian, Against Praxeas 12 (ANF vol. 3)
greek_edition: Latin not opened. English only.
english: Nay, it was because He had already His Son close at His side, as a second Person, His own Word, and a third Person also, the Spirit in the Word, that He purposely adopted the plural phrase, Let us make.
translator: Peter Holmes
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (1885), via New Advent
what_it_says: Genesis plural 'Let us make' refers to Father, Son (Word) and Spirit.
limits: Scriptural proof of plurality; no metaphysical account of the relation of the persons.

ref: Tertullian, Against Praxeas 25 (ANF vol. 3)
greek_edition: Latin not opened. English only.
english: These Three are one essence, not one Person, as it is said, I and my Father are One, John 10:30, in respect of unity of substance not singularity of number.
translator: Peter Holmes
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (1885), via New Advent
what_it_says: The three are one essence (substance), not one person; John 10:30 is read as unity of substance.
limits: 'Degree, form, aspect' sounds modalist to Nicene critics; Tertullian's Latin 'persona' and 'substantia' are not checked here. Hippolytus's 'two persons' is parallel but not identical.

ref: Origen, De Principiis I.2.1-2 (ANF vol. 4, Crombie; from Rufinus's Latin)
greek_edition: Greek not extant for this passage; the Latin (Rufinus) underlies the English. English only.
english: Wherefore we have always held that God is the Father of His only-begotten Son, who was born indeed of Him, and derives from Him what He is, but without any beginning... And therefore we must believe that Wisdom was generated before any beginning that can be either comprehended or expressed.
translator: Frederick Crombie (ANF vol. 4, translated from Latin)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4 (1885), via New Advent
what_it_says: The Son is eternally generated from the Father without beginning, 'Wisdom' and 'Word'.
limits: English is from Rufinus's Latin, not Origen's Greek; Origen's subordinationist passages elsewhere in De Principiis are not checked here.

ref: Novatian, On the Trinity 31 (ANF vol. 5, Wallis)
greek_edition: Latin not opened. English only.
english: He, then, when the Father willed it, proceeded from the Father, and He who was in the Father came forth from the Father; ... Assuredly God proceeding from God, causing a person second to the Father as being the Son, but not taking from the Father that characteristic that He is one God.
translator: Robert Ernest Wallis
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5 (1886), via New Advent
what_it_says: The Son always in the Father, proceeded when the Father willed; 'God proceeding from God' and still one God.
limits: Novatian also says the Father 'precedes' the Son 'in a certain sense', and calls the Son 'less' in some respect; subordinationist strands remain. Latin not checked.

ref: Basil, Letter 236 s.6 (NPNF2 vol. 8, Blomfield Jackson)
greek_edition: Greek terms οὐσία and ὑπόστασις only, as they appear in the New Advent English page; PG 32 not consulted.
english: The distinction between ousia and hypostasis is the same as that between the general and the particular... Wherefore, in the case of the Godhead, we confess one essence or substance ... but we confess a particular hypostasis.
translator: Blomfield Jackson
edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 8 (1895), via New Advent
what_it_says: Ousia is the general (one essence), hypostasis the particular (each Person); one Godhead, three hypostases.
limits: Post-Nicene (c. 375) terminology; Hippolytus uses prosopon, not hypostasis, for the persons, so the answer is a later clarification and not Hippolytus's own metaphysics.

ref: Gregory Nazianzen, Theological Oration 31 (Fifth) s.XIV (NPNF2 vol. 7)
greek_edition: Greek not consulted (SC 250). English only.
english: When then we look at the Godhead, or the First Cause, or the Monarchia, that which we conceive is One; but when we look at the Persons in Whom the Godhead dwells... there are Three Whom we worship.
translator: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow
edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 7 (1894), via New Advent
what_it_says: Looking at the Godhead or Monarchia we conceive one; looking at the Persons we worship three.
limits: Late-4th-century language; it answers the objection 'two persons = two gods' that Hippolytus CN 14 raises, but the Greek term (prosopa or hypostaseis) is not checked here.

ref: Augustine, On the Trinity XV.14.23 (NPNF1 vol. 3, Haddan)
greek_edition: Latin (Migne PL 42) not opened. English only.
english: The Word of God, then, the only-begotten Son of the Father, in all things like and equal to the Father, God of God, Light of Light, Wisdom of Wisdom, Essence of Essence, is altogether that which the Father is, yet is not the Father, because the one is Son, the other is Father. [...] as though uttering Himself, the Father begot the Word equal to Himself in all things.
translator: Arthur West Haddan
edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, vol. 3 (1887), via New Advent
what_it_says: The Word is equal to the Father in all things: God of God, Light of Light, Essence of Essence, begotten as the Father utters Himself.
limits: Augustine's 'as though uttering Himself' is the psychological analogy; it answers Hippolytus's 'uttering the voice first ... begetting Him as Light of Light' (CN 10) with eternal generation and equality.

ref: Nicene Creed (325/381), phrase 'God of God, Light of Light'
greek_edition: Creed text not retrieved (CCEL and New Advent pages tried; not found). Phrase quoted from memory.
edition: Nicene Creed (text not verified)
what_it_says: The Creed confesses the Son as God of God, Light of Light, and begotten not made.
limits: Not verified against a source page in this session.
memory_only: God of God, Light of Light, begotten, not made (Nicene Creed phrase; the Greek Theon ek Theou, Phos ek Photos).

ref: Aquinas, ST I q.27 a.1 corpus (procession in God)
greek_edition: Latin not opened. English only.
english: Divine Scripture uses, in relation to God, names which signify procession. This procession has been differently understood. Some have understood it in the sense of an effect, proceeding from its cause; so Arius took it, saying that the Son proceeds from the Father as His primary creature... Others take this procession to mean the cause proceeding to the effect... in which sense it was understood by Sabellius.
translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province (Summa, as on New Advent)
edition: Summa Theologiae I q.27 (New Advent transcription); publisher not checked
what_it_says: Procession in God is not creaturely emanation (Arius) nor mere modal manifestation (Sabellius).
limits: Scholastic framework (Aquinas) for the 'Logos went forth' problem; Hippolytus's CN 10 does not use these categories.

ref: Aquinas, ST I q.27 a.2 corpus (generation)
greek_edition: Latin not opened. English only.
english: The procession of the Word in God is called generation. [...] generation includes... a procession by way of similitude in the same specific nature; as a man proceeds from a man, and a horse from a horse.
translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province (Summa, as on New Advent)
edition: Summa Theologiae I q.27 (New Advent)
what_it_says: The Word's procession is generation, proper to a living principle with a similitude of nature.
limits: Analogy from living beings (the Summa applies generation by similitude of nature); the Latin is not checked.

ref: Aquinas, ST I q.34 a.1 (Word as personal name)
greek_edition: Latin not opened. English only.
english: The name of Word in God, if taken in its proper sense, is a personal name, and in no way an essential name. [...] Hence the term 'Word,' according as we use the term strictly of God, is to be taken as said not essentially, but personally.
translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province (Summa, as on New Advent)
edition: Summa Theologiae I q.34 (New Advent)
what_it_says: Word is a personal name of the Son, signifying what proceeds from another.
limits: Scholastic; Arian reading of 'Word' addressed in reply 1.

ref: Aquinas, ST I q.34 a.2 ad 1 (Word substantial and hypostatic)
greek_edition: Latin not opened. English only.
english: the Word of God is substantial and has a hypostatic being; but other words [as our own] are activities of the soul.
translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province (Summa, as on New Advent)
page: article 2, reply to objection 1 (quoting Damascene, De Fide Orth. i, 18)
edition: Summa Theologiae I q.34 (New Advent)
what_it_says: The divine Word subsists; it is not an accident of God.
limits: Quotes John of Damascus; a later metaphysic than Hippolytus.

ref: Aquinas, ST I q.34 a.3 corpus (Word and creatures)
greek_edition: Latin not opened. English only.
english: Word implies relation to creatures. For God by knowing Himself, knows every creature. Now the word conceived in the mind is representative of everything that is actually understood... His one only Word is expressive not only of the Father, but of all creatures.
translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province (Summa, as on New Advent)
edition: Summa Theologiae I q.34 (New Advent)
what_it_says: The Word is the expression of all creatures as well as of the Father.
limits: Gives a non-creaturely reason for the Word's relation to creatures; relevant to CN 12-13 (Word made manifest).
